title: Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes)
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Expression of Ideas
summary: Student-notes questions made easy: read the goal first, check every part of it, and avoid the true-but-off-goal trap — goal types, four worked examples and a 10-question practice quiz.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Rhetorical synthesis questions belong to **Expression of Ideas**, about 20% of the scored Reading and Writing questions (usually 8–12, shared with transitions). They are usually the **last questions in each module**, so you meet them when time is short — good news, because with the right method they are some of the fastest points on the test.

Instead of a normal passage, you see a list of **bullet-point notes** that a student has taken while researching a topic. The question names a **goal**, for example: "The student wants to **emphasize a similarity between the two dams**" or "The student wants to **introduce the qanat to an audience unfamiliar with it**." Then comes the fixed stem: **"Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?"** The four choices are sentences built from the notes.

Here is the secret: **almost every choice is true** according to the notes. The question is not "Which sentence is correct?" but "Which sentence does **this exact job**?" This is a writing-purpose question, not a reading-comprehension question.
The method: goal first, notes last

items: **Skip the notes. Go straight to the question and read the goal.** The goal is the only thing that decides the answer.

**Break the goal into parts.** "Emphasize / the difference / in length / between the two dams" has four parts. "Introduce / qanats / to an audience unfamiliar with them" means: name it + say what it is.
**Predict what the right sentence must contain.** For a difference: both things + a contrast word (while, whereas, unlike, but) + the feature named in the goal.

**Check every choice against every part of the goal.** Cross out any choice that misses even one part: only one of the two things, the wrong feature, a similarity instead of a difference, no explanation for a new audience.
**Use the notes only to break a tie or check accuracy.** If two choices seem to fit, look back at the notes to see which one uses the information correctly.

blocks.title: السر في السؤال ده
items: ما تقراش الملاحظات (notes) في الأول خالص. اقرأ الهدف (The student wants to…) وقسّمه أجزاء.
كل الاختيارات تقريبًا صح من ناحية المعلومات، بس واحد بس اللي بيحقق الهدف بالظبط. الاختيار «الصح بس مش في الموضوع» هو الفخ.
لو الهدف «تشابه» لازم تلاقي الحاجتين + كلمة زي both أو like. لو «اختلاف» لازم الحاجتين + while أو unlike.

blocks.text: Goal types and what the right answer must contain

rows: emphasize a **similarity** between X and Y
mention BOTH X and Y and the feature they share
both, like, similarly, also, as… as
a difference, or only X
emphasize a **difference / contrast** between X and Y

while, whereas, unlike, but, however, than

use the name without basic definitions, focus on the new point in the goal

found, showed, revealed, discovered
method only, or aim only

the results

say what the researchers are trying to do
to, in order to, aim, hope to
results or background

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1: emphasize a similarity**
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE.
It was built mainly from limestone blocks.
El Castillo is a pyramid in Mexico built by the Maya more than 3,000 years later.
El Castillo is also built mainly from limestone.
The Great Pyramid originally had smooth sides, while El Castillo has a staircase on each of its four sides.

blocks.text: **The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two pyramids. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?**

items: A) The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE, while El Castillo was built more than 3,000 years later.
B) Both the Great Pyramid of Giza and El Castillo were built mainly from limestone.
C) El Castillo, a Maya pyramid in Mexico, has a staircase on each of its four sides.
D) Unlike the Great Pyramid, which originally had smooth sides, El Castillo has four staircases.

blocks.title: Answer: B
items: Goal parts: similarity + both pyramids. Only B names both pyramids AND a shared feature (limestone), with the signal word "Both".
A is wrong: true, but it shows a difference in dates (true but off-goal).
C is wrong: it describes only one pyramid (half the goal).
D is wrong: it is a difference, signalled by "Unlike" (opposite of the goal).

blocks.text: **Worked example 2: introduce to an unfamiliar audience**
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items: Tahtib is a traditional Egyptian martial art performed with a long wooden stick.
Scenes resembling tahtib appear in ancient Egyptian tomb art.
Today it is often performed at weddings and festivals in Upper Egypt, usually accompanied by music.
In 2016, UNESCO added tahtib to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

blocks.text: **The student wants to introduce tahtib to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?**

items: A) Tahtib, which appears in ancient Egyptian tomb art, was added to a UNESCO list in 2016.
B) In 2016, tahtib joined UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
C) Tahtib, a traditional Egyptian martial art performed with a long wooden stick, is often seen at weddings and festivals in Upper Egypt.
D) Tahtib is often performed with music at weddings and festivals.

blocks.title: Answer: C
items: An unfamiliar reader first needs to know WHAT tahtib is. Only C explains it ("a traditional Egyptian martial art performed with a long wooden stick").
A is wrong: it gives history and an award but never says what tahtib is — the reader could think it is a painting or a song.
B is wrong: same problem; the name is used with no explanation.
D is wrong: "performed with music" could describe a dance or a song; it does not say it is a martial art.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3: present a study and its findings**
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items: In 2023, a team led by ecologist Mai Ibrahim studied 40 school gardens in Cairo.
The team counted the butterfly species that visited each garden over one year.
Gardens planted with native flowering plants attracted an average of 14 butterfly species.
Gardens planted mostly with imported ornamental plants attracted an average of 6 species.

blocks.text: **The student wants to present the study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?**

items: A) In a 2023 study of 40 Cairo school gardens, Mai Ibrahim's team found that gardens with native flowering plants attracted more than twice as many butterfly species (14 on average) as gardens with mostly imported plants (6).
B) Mai Ibrahim's team counted the butterfly species that visited 40 school gardens in Cairo over the course of one year.
C) Butterflies visit school gardens in Cairo that contain native plants and gardens that contain imported plants.
D) Gardens planted mostly with imported ornamental plants attracted an average of six butterfly species.

blocks.title: Answer: A
items: The goal has two parts: the study (who, what) AND its findings (the result). Only A gives both, and its comparison (14 vs 6 = more than twice) matches the notes.
B is wrong: it presents the study's method but not the findings (half the goal).
C is wrong: it hides the finding; it says nothing about the difference between the gardens.
D is wrong: it gives one number from the results but no study and no comparison (half the goal).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4: a difference in one specific feature**
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items: Emperor penguins and Adélie penguins both live in Antarctica.
Emperor penguins can grow to more than one meter tall.
Adélie penguins grow to about 70 centimeters tall.
Emperor penguins breed during the Antarctic winter.
Adélie penguins breed during the Antarctic summer.

blocks.text: **The student wants to emphasize a difference in the breeding seasons of the two species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?**

items: A) Emperor penguins, which can grow to more than one meter tall, are much larger than Adélie penguins.
B) Both emperor penguins and Adélie penguins live and breed in Antarctica.
C) Emperor penguins breed during the Antarctic winter.
D) While emperor penguins breed during the harsh Antarctic winter, Adélie penguins breed in the summer.

blocks.title: Answer: D
items: Goal parts: difference + breeding season + both species. D has all three, with the contrast word "While".
A is the classic trap: it is a difference between the two species, but in SIZE, not breeding season (true but off-goal).
B is wrong: it shows a similarity.
C is wrong: it mentions only one species, so no difference is shown (half the goal).

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **True but off-goal:** the sentence is accurate and well written but does a different job (a difference in size when the goal asks about breeding seasons).
**Half the goal:** only one of two things, or the study without its findings, or the method without the results.
**Reversed goal:** a similarity when the goal asks for a difference, or the opposite.
**The name with no explanation:** for an unfamiliar audience, a choice that only uses the name fails, however interesting its facts.
**Over-explaining for a familiar audience:** a choice that defines something the audience already knows is wasting the sentence.
**The biggest-sentence trap:** the longest choice with the most facts is not automatically right. Relevance beats quantity.
**Reading the notes first:** you waste time and start judging choices by interest, not by the goal.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Jump to the question line and read the goal. Underline (in your head) the key words: similarity, difference, introduce, unfamiliar, findings, method, aim, when and where.
Predict the shape of the answer: both + both/like; both + while/unlike; name + "a/an…" description; study + found.
Eliminate choices by the goal alone. You will often answer without reading the notes at all.
Check the notes only if two choices are left.
These questions usually come last in the module: keep 4–5 minutes for them, roughly 40–60 seconds each.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Rhetorical Synthesis — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 10 questions in Digital SAT format. Untimed: read the goal first, break it into parts, and only then check the choices — and the notes if you need them.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Psychologist Laila Hosny wanted to know whether handwriting notes helps students remember lectures.
• In 2024, she asked 120 university students to watch the same recorded lecture.
• Half the students took notes by hand; the other half typed notes on laptops.
• One week later, the handwriting group scored 18 percent higher on a quiz about the lecture.
questions.q: The student wants to describe the methodology of Hosny's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Hosny found that students who took notes by hand scored 18 percent higher on a quiz one week later.
Hosny wanted to know whether handwriting notes helps students remember lectures.
Hosny had 120 university students watch the same lecture, with half taking notes by hand and half typing them on laptops.
Taking notes by hand may help students remember lectures better than typing them.
questions.e: Methodology = how the study was done. Only C describes the participants and the procedure. A gives the finding, B the aim, and D a conclusion.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ibn al-Haytham was an Arab scholar born in Basra around 965 CE.
• He studied how light travels and how the eye sees.
• He tested his ideas through careful experiments, such as observing light passing through a small hole into a dark room.
• Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist born in 1564.
• Galileo also tested his ideas through experiments, for example by rolling balls down sloping ramps.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Ibn al-Haytham and Galileo. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Like Galileo centuries later, Ibn al-Haytham tested his ideas through careful experiments.
Ibn al-Haytham was born around 965 CE, about six hundred years before Galileo.
Galileo, an Italian scientist, rolled balls down sloping ramps to test his ideas.
Ibn al-Haytham, an Arab scholar from Basra, studied how light travels and how the eye sees.
questions.e: A names both scientists and the shared feature (testing ideas through experiments) with "Like". B shows a difference in dates; C and D mention only one scientist.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Camels can go several days without drinking in hot weather.
• A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
• Camels' red blood cells are oval rather than round.
• This shape lets the cells keep flowing through blood vessels even when the camel is badly dehydrated.
• A thirsty camel can drink more than 100 liters of water in a short time.
questions.q: The student wants to explain one way a camel's body is adapted to survive dehydration. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: A camel's hump stores fat rather than water, as many people wrongly believe.
Because their red blood cells are oval, camels' blood keeps flowing even when the animals are badly dehydrated.
Camels can go several days without drinking in hot weather.
Camels can go several days without water, and their humps store fat.
questions.e: The goal asks for an explanation (how the body copes), so it needs a cause or mechanism. B gives one: oval cells keep blood flowing. A corrects a myth, and C and D state facts without explaining how the camel survives.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Old Aswan Dam was completed in 1902.
• The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.
• Both dams are on the Nile at Aswan, in southern Egypt.
• The High Dam created Lake Nasser, one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.
• The Old Aswan Dam is about 1.9 kilometers long; the High Dam is about 3.8 kilometers long.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize the difference in length between the two dams. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Both dams were built on the Nile at Aswan, in southern Egypt.
The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, created Lake Nasser.
The Old Aswan Dam was completed in 1902, almost seventy years before the High Dam.
At about 3.8 kilometers long, the Aswan High Dam is roughly twice the length of the 1.9-kilometer Old Aswan Dam.
questions.e: Only D compares the two dams' lengths. C is a difference too, but in dates, not length (true but off-goal); A is a similarity, and B mentions one dam.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, in 1896.
• About 240 athletes from 14 nations took part.
• All of the athletes at those first Games were men.
• Women competed in the Olympic Games for the first time in 1900, in Paris.
questions.q: The student wants to indicate when and where the first modern Olympic Games were held. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens, Greece, in 1896.
About 240 athletes from 14 nations competed in the first modern Olympic Games.
Women first competed in the Olympic Games in 1900.
The 1900 Olympic Games, held in Paris, were the first to include women athletes.
questions.e: A gives both the time (1896) and the place (Athens) of the first modern Games. B gives neither; C gives only a date of a different event; D gives a date and place but for the wrong Games.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A qanat is an underground channel that carries water from a hillside aquifer to fields and villages.
• Qanats rely on gravity, so they need no pumps.
• The technology developed in ancient Persia.
• Qanats were later built in several places, including Egypt's Kharga Oasis.
• Some qanats are still in use today.
questions.q: The student wants to introduce qanats to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Qanats, which developed in ancient Persia, were later built in Egypt's Kharga Oasis.
Developed in ancient Persia, qanats are underground channels that use gravity to carry water from hillside aquifers to fields and villages.
Some qanats are still in use today, long after they were first built.
Because qanats rely on gravity, they need no pumps.
questions.e: A new audience needs to know what a qanat is, and only B defines it (underground channels that carry water). A, C and D use the name without saying what a qanat actually is.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Some birds use tools to obtain food.
• New Caledonian crows shape twigs into hooks to pull insects out of tree bark.
• Egyptian vultures drop stones onto ostrich eggs to crack them open.
• Woodpecker finches in the Galápagos Islands use cactus spines to dig insect larvae out of wood.
• Researchers point out that tool use is not limited to mammals such as chimpanzees.
questions.q: The student wants to make a generalization about tool use in birds. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: New Caledonian crows shape twigs into hooks to pull insects out of tree bark.
Egyptian vultures drop stones onto ostrich eggs, while woodpecker finches dig out larvae with cactus spines.
Several bird species, not only mammals such as chimpanzees, use tools to obtain food.
Woodpecker finches, which live in the Galápagos Islands, use cactus spines as tools.
questions.e: A generalization is a broad statement about the group, which C gives ("Several bird species… use tools"). A, B and D are specific examples, not generalizations.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hassan Fathy (1900–1989) was an Egyptian architect.
• In the 1940s, he designed the village of New Gourna near Luxor.
• He built with mud brick, a cheap local material, and used traditional forms such as domes and vaults.
• His book Architecture for the Poor describes the New Gourna project.
questions.q: The student wants to introduce Hassan Fathy and his work to an audience unfamiliar with him. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Hassan Fathy wrote Architecture for the Poor, a book about the New Gourna project.
Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy designed New Gourna, a village near Luxor built from mud brick in the 1940s.
New Gourna, near Luxor, features domes and vaults made of mud brick.
In the 1940s, Hassan Fathy used mud brick and traditional forms such as domes and vaults.
questions.e: B tells a new reader who Fathy was (an Egyptian architect) and what his work was. A and D never say he was an architect, and C does not mention Fathy at all.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Engineers at a university in Alexandria are developing a new coating for fishing nets.
• The coating is made from crushed shrimp shells.
• Its purpose is to stop algae and small shellfish from growing on the nets.
• Nets covered with algae become heavy and must be replaced often, which costs fishers money.
• In early tests, coated nets stayed clean three times longer than uncoated nets.
questions.q: The student wants to state the aim of the engineers' work. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: In early tests, the coated nets stayed clean three times longer than uncoated nets.
The engineers' new coating is made from crushed shrimp shells.
Nets covered with algae become heavy and must be replaced often.
Engineers in Alexandria are developing a shrimp-shell coating to keep algae and shellfish from growing on fishing nets.
questions.e: The aim is what the engineers are trying to achieve, shown in D by "to keep algae and shellfish from growing". A gives a result, B the material, and C background on the problem.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Rosetta Stone is a slab of dark granodiorite about 1.1 meters tall.
• It was found in 1799 near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile Delta.
• It records the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and ancient Greek.
• Because scholars could read the Greek, the stone became the key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs.
• It is now displayed at the British Museum in London.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize the significance of the Rosetta Stone to an audience already familiar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Because it records the same decree in Greek as well as in hieroglyphs, the Rosetta Stone became the key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs.
The Rosetta Stone, a slab of dark granodiorite, is about 1.1 meters tall.
The Rosetta Stone is now displayed at the British Museum in London.
The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 near the town of Rashid in the Nile Delta.
questions.e: Significance = why it matters: A explains that the stone unlocked hieroglyphs, without basic background the familiar audience does not need. B, C and D give physical details, location and discovery, not significance.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Read the goal before the notes; the goal alone decides the answer.
Check every part of the goal: both items, the right feature, the right audience, study + findings.
Most choices are true — the trap is a true sentence that does a different job.
Unfamiliar audience → name + explanation. Familiar audience → no basic definition needed.
Similarity → both / like. Difference → while / unlike / than.
